AlberdiLab | hilldiv3 manuscript Microflora Danica worked example: data and diversity Alberdi Lab Last update: 2026-11-04 Chapter 1 Introduction This webbook contains the data and reproducible code for the Microflora Danica worked example in the hilldiv3 manuscript. The selected panel contains sample and genome metadata, a representative MAG abundance matrix, and a phylogenetic tree. The chapters describe the panel and begin neutral and phylogenetic diversity analyses. 1.1 Prepare the R environment 1.1.1 Environment Clone the GitHub repository and open hilldiv3-ms.Rproj, or create a new RStudio project from: https://github.com/alberdilab/hilldiv3-ms.git 1.1.2 Libraries The book uses these R packages: library(data.table) library(ape) library(knitr) library(ggplot2) library(maps) library(hilldiv3) stopifnot(utils::packageVersion("hilldiv3") >= "3.1.0.9000") 1.2 Analysis steps 1.2.1 Step 0 - Data preparation The data preparation chapter describes the committed Microflora Danica panel, loads it, and checks its sample, genome, abundance, and tree alignment. The source-download and preparation scripts are in scripts/. 1.2.2 Step 1 - Data overview The data overview chapter summarizes sample coverage, sampling dates, geography, and representative genomes. 1.2.3 Step 2 - Initial diversity analyses The diversity analyses chapter calculates neutral and phylogenetic Hill numbers at orders 0, 1, and 2, traces diversity profiles across orders, then partitions diversity within and between the eight habitat classes. The hilldiv3 calls appear in highlighted code blocks. 1.2.4 Step 3 - Pairwise beta diversity The pairwise beta diversity chapter compares every pair of samples with neutral and phylogenetic Hill-number C dissimilarity. It summarizes within- and between-habitat pairs and shows habitat heatmaps and sample-level ordinations at \(q=0\) and \(q=1\). The hillpair() calls are shown before the code that formats their results. 1.2.5 Step 4 - Taxonomic shares and contributions The taxonomic shares chapter uses hillshare() to allocate neutral and phylogenetic Hill power sums to four named phyla and the remaining representatives. A focused agricultural field versus natural grassland soil comparison shows how a nearly stable Actinomycetota share conceals opposing Gaiellales and Streptosporangiales patterns. hillcontrib() then attributes the same neutral and phylogenetic dissimilarities to the phyla and these orders.

Chapter 2 Data preparation The staged panel contains 360 geographically dispersed Microflora Danica samples: 45 from each of eight habitat classes. It uses the same locked sample and representative genome selections as the gifter case study. 2.1 Input data File Contents data/mag_relative_abundance.tsv.xz Relative abundances for 5,518 representative MAGs (rows) and 360 samples (columns). The first column is genome_id. data/sample_metadata.tsv Sample metadata in abundance-column order, including habitat class, ontology, location, date, and selection audit. data/representative_metadata.tsv Metadata for the 95% ANI species representatives in abundance-row order. data/representative_tree.nwk Source tree pruned to the 5,518 representative genome_id tips, retaining source branch lengths. 2.2 Load the staged panel The committed tables and tree are the inputs to the following chapters. Load them from the repository root: sample_metadata <- data.table::fread( "data/sample_metadata.tsv", data.table = FALSE ) genome_metadata <- data.table::fread( "data/representative_metadata.tsv", data.table = FALSE ) genome_abundance <- data.table::fread( cmd = "xz -dc data/mag_relative_abundance.tsv.xz", data.table = FALSE, check.names = FALSE ) genome_tree <- ape::read.tree("data/representative_tree.nwk") The selected panel has 45 samples in each habitat class: habitats <- table(sample_metadata$habitat_label) knitr::kable( data.frame(habitat = names(habitats), samples = as.integer(habitats)), col.names = c("Habitat", "Samples") ) Habitat Samples Agricultural field soil 45 Natural bog/fen soil 45 Natural forest soil 45 Natural freshwater sediment 45 Natural grassland soil 45 Natural saltwater sediment 45 Urban greenspace soil 45 Urban wastewater water 45 2.3 Check the staged objects The abundance rows and columns must align with the metadata, and the tree must contain exactly the representative genomes: stopifnot( nrow(sample_metadata) == 360L, nrow(genome_metadata) == 5518L, nrow(genome_abundance) == 5518L, ncol(genome_abundance) == 361L, length(habitats) == 8L, all(habitats == 45L), identical(genome_abundance$genome_id, genome_metadata$genome_id), identical(names(genome_abundance)[-1L], sample_metadata$sample_id), setequal(genome_tree$tip.label, genome_metadata$genome_id) ) profile_totals <- colSums(as.matrix(genome_abundance[-1L])) stopifnot(all(is.finite(profile_totals)), all(profile_totals > 0.99 & profile_totals < 1.01)) cat(sprintf( "%d samples, %d representative genomes, %d tree tips; profile sums %.6f–%.6f.\n", nrow(sample_metadata), nrow(genome_metadata), ape::Ntip(genome_tree), min(profile_totals), max(profile_totals) )) 360 samples, 5518 representative genomes, 5518 tree tips; profile sums 0.999988–1.000015. The abundance values are proportions of the published MFD MAG profile, not genome or read counts. The preparation script keeps strain (t__) rows from the Sylph profiles, maps MAGs to their published secondary_cluster, sums each 95% ANI cluster, and divides percentages by 100. It assigns each cluster profile to the deposited representative MAG. It does not renormalize profiles. The representative abundance therefore stands for its cluster; it does not imply that all members have identical gene content. These values describe the MFD MAG profile, not the fraction of all DNA in each sample. 2.4 Sources The primary study is Singleton and colleagues, The Microflora Danica atlas of Danish environmental microbiomes. The Microflora Danica data deposit provides Nitrifiers.tar.gz, including the published MAG metadata and Sylph abundance table. Please cite both the study and deposit when using these data, and consult the deposit for its reuse terms. The sample and representative tables are copies of the locked panels at gifter commit f04f7de. The source tree is gtdb-shallow.tree from the MFD companion repository at commit 957591d. Tips outside the representative panel were removed. 2.5 Rebuild and verify The committed files are ready to use. To rebuild them from the pinned public sources, install R packages data.table and ape, then run: bash scripts/fetch-source-data.sh Rscript scripts/prepare-data.R Rscript scripts/check-data.R The source archive is about 228 MB. Downloads remain in the ignored sources/ directory. The preparation script also accepts paths to existing MAG metadata, abundance TSV.xz, and source tree files, in that order. To verify the committed snapshot byte for byte: shasum -a 256 -c data/SHA256SUMS The checker verifies sample and genome IDs, 45 samples per habitat, table ordering, finite nonnegative abundances, near-unit profile sums, and exact tree-tip identity. In this snapshot, sample profile totals range from 0.999988 to 1.000015.

Chapter 4 Initial diversity analyses We use hilldiv3 to describe diversity in the selected panel. Neutral Hill numbers use representative relative abundances; phylogenetic Hill numbers also use the pruned representative tree. We evaluate diversity orders \(q=0\) (all detected units receive full weight), \(q=1\) (abundance-weighted diversity), and \(q=2\) (common units weighted more strongly). For neutral diversity, \(q=0\) is the count of detected representatives. Functional diversity awaits a matched trait or gene-function table. 4.1 Within-sample diversity hilldiv() calculates one diversity type per call. The tree and pooled reference depth are supplied only for phylogenetic diversity. alpha_neutral <- hilldiv3::hilldiv( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), type = "neutral" ) alpha_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hilldiv( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", reference = "pool" ) For the plots and table below, the results are joined to habitat labels. ggplot2::ggplot(alpha_diversity, ggplot2::aes(x = value, y = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.55, fill = "#e6c7c7", colour = "#702626") + ggplot2::geom_jitter(height = 0.13, width = 0, alpha = 0.28, size = 0.65, colour = "#702626") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(type, order), ncol = 3, scales = "free_x") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Hill diversity", y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Hill numbers for 45 samples in each habitat class. Boxes show medians and interquartile ranges; points are individual samples. Horizontal scales differ by panel. q1 <- alpha_diversity[alpha_diversity$q == 1, ] q1_summary <- aggregate( value ~ habitat + type, data = q1, FUN = function(x) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", median(x), unname(quantile(x, 0.25)), unname(quantile(x, 0.75))) ) q1_neutral <- q1_summary[q1_summary$type == "Neutral", c("habitat", "value")] q1_phylo <- q1_summary[q1_summary$type == "Phylogenetic", c("habitat", "value")] names(q1_neutral)[2] <- "Neutral q = 1" names(q1_phylo)[2] <- "Phylogenetic q = 1" q1_table <- merge(q1_neutral, q1_phylo, by = "habitat", sort = FALSE) q1_table <- q1_table[match(habitat_levels, q1_table$habitat), ] names(q1_table)[1] <- "Habitat" rownames(q1_table) <- NULL knitr::kable(q1_table, row.names = FALSE) Habitat Neutral q = 1 Phylogenetic q = 1 Agricultural field soil 47.8 [41.2–58.8] 4.9 [4.5–5.1] Natural grassland soil 55.1 [38.9–67.3] 4.5 [4.1–5.0] Natural forest soil 74.5 [47.9–107.0] 4.8 [4.3–5.3] Urban greenspace soil 48.4 [39.1–64.9] 4.8 [4.4–5.1] Natural bog/fen soil 52.7 [35.6–67.6] 4.4 [3.8–5.1] Natural freshwater sediment 50.6 [32.8–73.2] 5.4 [4.3–6.2] Natural saltwater sediment 48.3 [37.4–65.7] 4.7 [3.9–5.1] Urban wastewater water 78.0 [66.6–93.6] 7.9 [7.3–8.5] Median [interquartile range] of \(q=1\) diversity by habitat. At \(q=1\), median neutral diversity ranges from 47.8 in Agricultural field soil to 78.0 in Urban wastewater water. The phylogenetic values use hilldiv3’s common pooled reference tree depth, so samples are evaluated on the same scale. Their numerical values should be compared within the phylogenetic panels, rather than interpreted as counts of MAGs. Neutral \(q=0\) is the number of representatives with a positive reported abundance; it is sensitive to very small values in the source profiles. 4.2 Diversity profiles across orders hillprof() extends the three selected orders to a finer sweep. To keep the comparison readable, each habitat profile below is the mean of its 45 sample abundance vectors. These are descriptive pooled profiles; their \(q=0\) values count representatives detected in any of those samples. profile_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillprof( habitat_profiles, q = seq(0, 2, by = 0.25), type = "neutral" ) profile_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillprof( habitat_profiles, q = seq(0, 2, by = 0.25), tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", reference = "pool" ) ggplot2::ggplot(profiles, ggplot2::aes(x = q, y = value, colour = sample)) + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors( length(habitat_levels), palette = "Dark 3")) + ggplot2::scale_y_log10() + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_y") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Diversity order (q)", y = "Hill diversity (log scale)", colour = "Habitat") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Diversity profiles of the mean abundance vector in each habitat. The two panels use separate vertical scales; values should be compared within a panel. The neutral ranking changes with order: bog/fen soil has the highest pooled richness at \(q=0\), while forest soil has the highest diversity at \(q=1\) and \(q=2\). This illustrates why a single diversity order does not capture every aspect of a profile. 4.3 Partitioning across habitats The next calculation partitions diversity across individual samples, habitat classes, and the complete panel. At each step, hilldiv3 reports a beta factor: the effective number of distinct units added at that scale. The two beta factors multiply to give the total gamma-to-alpha ratio. Each sample has equal weight; the design has 45 samples in every habitat class. hillpart() uses the habitat metadata to partition diversity across the sample-to-habitat and habitat-to-panel scales. partition_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillpart( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), hierarchy = ~ habitat_class, metadata = habitat_metadata, type = "neutral" ) partition_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillpart( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), tree = genome_tree, hierarchy = ~ habitat_class, metadata = habitat_metadata, type = "phylogenetic" ) partition_neutral <- plain_hill_result(partition_neutral) partition_phylogenetic <- plain_hill_result(partition_phylogenetic) partition_neutral$type <- "Neutral" partition_phylogenetic$type <- "Phylogenetic" partition <- rbind(partition_neutral, partition_phylogenetic) stopifnot(all(is.finite(partition$diversity)), all(is.finite(partition$beta[partition$scale != "sample"]))) within <- partition[partition$scale == "habitat_class", c("type", "q", "beta")] between <- partition[partition$scale == "total", c("type", "q", "beta", "diversity")] names(within)[3] <- "Within habitats" names(between)[3:4] <- c("Between habitats", "Gamma diversity") partition_table <- merge(within, between, by = c("type", "q"), sort = FALSE) partition_table <- partition_table[order(match(partition_table$type, c("Neutral", "Phylogenetic")), partition_table$q), ] knitr::kable(partition_table, digits = 2) type q Within habitats Between habitats Gamma diversity Neutral 0 7.50 3.66 3552.00 Neutral 1 5.04 3.33 893.78 Neutral 2 4.80 2.76 334.78 Phylogenetic 0 4.17 3.29 611.03 Phylogenetic 1 1.46 1.56 21.51 Phylogenetic 2 1.12 1.12 6.19 Hierarchical Hill-number partition. Beta factors describe sample-to-habitat and habitat-to-panel turnover; gamma is diversity in the full panel. At \(q=1\), neutral beta diversity is 5.04 from samples to habitats and 3.33 from habitats to the full panel. The corresponding phylogenetic factors are 1.46 and 1.56. These are descriptive comparisons of a geographically selected panel. Habitat and collection year are not independently balanced, so these summaries do not by themselves establish habitat effects. Relative abundances also cannot support read-count rarefaction or sampling-depth uncertainty estimates.

Chapter 5 Pairwise beta diversity The diversity chapter partitions turnover across the whole panel. Here we compare every pair of the 360 samples with hilldiv3::hillpair(). For each pair, we use the C dissimilarity, the complement of the C overlap derived from multiplicative Hill beta diversity. It ranges from zero for identical communities to one for no overlap. We calculate neutral and phylogenetic values at \(q=0\), \(q=1\), and \(q=2\) using the same representative profiles and tree as above. Each type and order has 64,620 unique sample pairs. The two hillpair() calls return one row per sample pair and order. We request the long-format result so the sample IDs can be joined to their habitats. pair_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillpair( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), metric = "C", type = "neutral", out = "tibble" ) pair_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillpair( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), metric = "C", tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", out = "tibble" ) 5.1 Within and between habitats The table summarizes all sample pairs in each category. A habitat contributes 990 within-habitat pairs; two distinct habitats contribute 2,025 pairs. These pairs share samples, so their values are descriptive observations rather than independent replicates for a significance test. pair_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply( split(pairwise, list(pairwise$type, pairwise$q, pairwise$comparison), drop = TRUE), function(d) data.frame( Type = as.character(d$type[1]), q = d$q[1], Comparison = d$comparison[1], Pairs = nrow(d), Median = median(d$value), Q1 = unname(quantile(d$value, 0.25)), Q3 = unname(quantile(d$value, 0.75)) ) )) pair_summary <- pair_summary[ order(match(pair_summary$Type, c("Neutral", "Phylogenetic")), pair_summary$q, match(pair_summary$Comparison, c("Within habitat", "Between habitats"))), ] pair_summary$`Median [IQR]` <- sprintf( "%.3f [%.3f–%.3f]", pair_summary$Median, pair_summary$Q1, pair_summary$Q3 ) knitr::kable(pair_summary[c("Type", "q", "Comparison", "Pairs", "Median [IQR]")], row.names = FALSE) Type q Comparison Pairs Median [IQR] Neutral 0 Within habitat 7920 0.714 [0.484–0.898] Neutral 0 Between habitats 56700 0.992 [0.872–1.000] Neutral 1 Within habitat 7920 0.748 [0.527–0.923] Neutral 1 Between habitats 56700 0.999 [0.902–1.000] Neutral 2 Within habitat 7920 0.842 [0.639–0.971] Neutral 2 Between habitats 56700 1.000 [0.950–1.000] Phylogenetic 0 Within habitat 7920 0.438 [0.297–0.576] Phylogenetic 0 Between habitats 56700 0.758 [0.570–0.843] Phylogenetic 1 Within habitat 7920 0.183 [0.115–0.285] Phylogenetic 1 Between habitats 56700 0.454 [0.258–0.545] Phylogenetic 2 Within habitat 7920 0.085 [0.043–0.155] Phylogenetic 2 Between habitats 56700 0.217 [0.124–0.300] C dissimilarity for all unique sample pairs, summarized as median [interquartile range]. At \(q=1\), neutral C dissimilarity has median 0.748 within habitats and 0.999 between habitats. At \(q=1\), phylogenetic C dissimilarity has median 0.183 within habitats and 0.454 between habitats. The matrices are symmetric. Saltwater sediment and wastewater are nearly maximally dissimilar to the soil habitats at \(q=1\) in the neutral analysis. Their phylogenetic dissimilarities are lower, showing that the sample pairs retain some shared evolutionary branch structure despite little overlap in representative profiles. 5.3 Sample-level ordination Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) projects the \(q=0\) and \(q=1\) dissimilarities into two dimensions. At \(q=0\), neutral dissimilarity reflects overlap among detected representatives; phylogenetic dissimilarity also accounts for their shared tree branches. We apply a Cailliez correction because C dissimilarity need not be Euclidean. Axis percentages refer to the corrected distance matrix in each panel. ggplot2::ggplot(ordination, ggplot2::aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, colour = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 1.3) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors( length(habitat_levels), palette = "Dark 3")) + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free") + ggplot2::labs(x = "PCoA 1", y = "PCoA 2", colour = "Habitat") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Each point is one sample. The top row shows richness-based \(q=0\) dissimilarity; the bottom row shows abundance-weighted \(q=1\) dissimilarity. Axis percentages are the shares of positive eigenvalues after the Cailliez correction; coordinates are comparable only within a panel. The pairwise patterns describe this selected panel. Pairs sharing samples are dependent, and habitat class is partly confounded with sampling year. We do not treat visual separation or differences between pairwise medians as a formal test of a habitat effect. As elsewhere, \(q=0\) responds to very small reported abundances in the source profiles.

Chapter 6 Taxonomic shares and dissimilarity contributions The diversity and pairwise beta diversity chapters describe whole communities. Here we use hilldiv3::hillshare() to allocate each sample’s Hill power sum to sets of representative MAGs. A share is a fraction between zero and one, not a fraction of the effective Hill number reported by hilldiv(). The calculation is descriptive; it does not test whether a phylum is enriched in a habitat. This chapter was rendered with hilldiv3 version 3.1.0.9000. 6.1 Define the genome sets We use four phyla that have substantial abundance or dissimilarity contributions in the field–grassland soil comparison. The Other set contains every remaining representative, so the five sets are disjoint and exhaustive. Each representative stands for its published 95% ANI cluster; the shares describe those cluster profiles, not the abundance of every MAG within a cluster. phylum <- sub("^p__", "", genome_metadata$phylum) focus_phyla <- c("Pseudomonadota", "Actinomycetota", "Acidobacteriota", "Thermoproteota") contrast_habitats <- c("Agricultural field soil", "Natural grassland soil") share_sets <- lapply(focus_phyla, function(name) { genome_metadata$genome_id[phylum == name] }) names(share_sets) <- focus_phyla share_sets$Other <- genome_metadata$genome_id[!phylum %in% focus_phyla] stopifnot(sum(lengths(share_sets)) == nrow(genome_metadata), setequal(unlist(share_sets, use.names = FALSE), genome_metadata$genome_id)) hillshare() returns one row for each sample, order, diversity type, and set. The phylogenetic call uses the same representative tree as the earlier chapters. Both diversity types are requested together. shares <- hilldiv3::hillshare( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), tree = genome_tree, type = c("neutral", "phylogenetic"), sets = share_sets ) 6.2 Shares across habitats The heatmap shows the median share among the 45 samples in each habitat. Its colour scale is the same in every panel. At neutral \(q=1\), a set’s share equals its summed relative abundance. At \(q=0\), each detected representative has equal neutral weight; at \(q=2\), abundant representatives carry more weight. Phylogenetic shares also allocate the weights of tree branches to their descendant representatives. ggplot2::ggplot(share_medians, ggplot2::aes(x = Habitat, y = Set, fill = share)) + ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) + ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient( low = "#f7f7f7", high = "#8b1e1e", limits = c(0, 1), labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x), name = "Median share" ) + ggplot2::facet_grid(Order ~ Type) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme( panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(), axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold") ) Median power-sum shares in each habitat. Medians are taken separately for each set, so the displayed medians need not sum to one; the five shares sum to one within every individual sample, type, and order. 6.3 A stable phylum total hides order turnover The broad habitat comparison in the Microflora Danica atlas places fields and grasslands among similar soil environments. Its supplementary genome analysis notes widespread Gaiella and a Trebonia species found in grasslands. We use the representative MAG profiles to ask whether similar abundance at the phylum level can conceal opposing changes among its members. The parent phylum’s share comes from the earlier hillshare() result. At neutral \(q=1\), each share equals that set’s summed abundance within the MFD MAG profile. We compare the mean abundance profiles of agricultural field soil and natural grassland soil, calculated earlier from 45 samples per habitat. Both are soils, but the source metadata classify one as agricultural and the other as natural. This gives the contribution analysis an ecological land-use question with a shared sample matrix. It is one comparison of two habitat mean vectors, not the median of the 2,025 individual sample pairs shown in the pairwise analysis. The samples are not matched on soil properties, vegetation, location, or sampling year, so this descriptive contrast cannot isolate an effect of human land use. The same five disjoint genome sets used for hillshare() cover every representative. Here hillcontrib() attributes the \(q=1\) C dissimilarity to those sets. A contribution is a part of the dissimilarity, whereas the earlier power-sum share describes one profile on its own. contrib_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", type = "neutral", sets = share_sets ) contrib_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", sets = share_sets ) ggplot2::ggplot(contributions, ggplot2::aes(x = Type, y = contribution, fill = set)) + ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.55) + ggplot2::coord_flip() + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous( limits = c(0, 0.3), breaks = seq(0, 0.3, by = 0.1), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0)) ) + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c( Pseudomonadota = "#702626", Actinomycetota = "#ca725c", Acidobacteriota = "#d8b763", Thermoproteota = "#1b6b75", Other = "#a6a6a6" )) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Contribution to C dissimilarity (q = 1)", fill = "Representative set") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) The bar lengths are the C dissimilarities for the same two mean profiles; their segments sum to those values. They are not median contributions among sample pairs. Neutral C dissimilarity is 0.285 and phylogenetic C dissimilarity is 0.048. Actinomycetota accounts for 37.9% of the neutral value and 35.3% of the phylogenetic value. Pseudomonadota and Thermoproteota also make substantial contributions. Phylogenetic attribution allocates shared branch turnover to descendant representatives under hillcontrib()’s specified rule; it is not a unique biological assignment of each branch to a phylum. 6.6.1 The orders behind the Actinomycetota contribution The phylum totals above do not show which Actinomycetota representatives create the difference. We now partition the same two habitat mean profiles into Gaiellales, Streptosporangiales, the remaining Actinomycetota, and all representatives outside the phylum. The four sets are disjoint and exhaustive, so their C contributions sum to the corresponding whole-community values. actino_contrib_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", type = "neutral", sets = actino_contrib_sets ) actino_contrib_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", sets = actino_contrib_sets ) ggplot2::ggplot(actino_contrib_plot, ggplot2::aes(x = Type, y = Fraction, fill = Set)) + ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.55) + ggplot2::coord_flip() + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous( limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25), labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0)) ) + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c( Gaiellales = "#9d2f30", Streptosporangiales = "#d4846e", `Remaining Actinomycetota` = "#a6a6a6" )) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of Actinomycetota C contribution", fill = "Representative set") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) The bars divide the Actinomycetota segment of the preceding figure, not the whole-community C value. Both use the same field and grassland mean profiles; these are not sample-pair medians. Gaiellales and Streptosporangiales together account for 50.2% of Actinomycetota’s neutral contribution and 52.8% of its phylogenetic contribution. Relative to the full C values, these two orders account for 19.1% and 18.6%, respectively. Thus the nearly unchanged phylum abundance does not imply that its constituent representatives are unchanged. The field and grassland samples differ in location, soil properties, sampling project, and year; these descriptive differences cannot be assigned to land management alone. 6.6.2 How phylogenetic weighting redistributes contributions Thermoproteota accounts for 9.1% of the neutral C value and 19.0% of the phylogenetic value. Pseudomonadota moves in the opposite direction, from 32.7% to 22.0% of the phylogenetic value. Representatives assigned to Nitrososphaerales make up 100.0% and 99.7% of Thermoproteota abundance in the field and grassland mean profiles, respectively. That is a taxonomic assignment, not a measurement of function. The contribution shares describe two different C values; no significance test is involved. The figure shows one small clade from each phylum on the same branch-gap colour scale. The nonlinear colour mapping keeps smaller nonzero gaps visible; the legend reports the original gap values. Each panel shows a separate four-MAG clade in the source tree. Horizontal branches are drawn to scale and coloured by the same length-weighted \(q=1\) abundance-gap scale, with nonlinear colour spacing; grey vertical lines connect them. Chapter 7 Functional diversity The previous chapters used abundances and a phylogeny. Here we add the functional layer: genome-inferred traits distilled from KEGG ortholog annotations of the same 5,518 representative MAGs. Each MAG has a completeness score between zero and one for every function-level trait in the distillR biosynthesis and degradation domains, such as nucleic acid biosynthesis or polysaccharide degradation. We turn these traits into a functional distance between MAGs and use it in hilldiv3 to calculate functional diversity and related metrics. 7.1 Functional traits scripts/distill-functional-traits.R distils the primary KEGG ortholog hit of every gene (Drakkar 2.6.9, KOfam database of 2026-07-02) into trait tables. We use the function level, which has one column per function and the same row order as the representative metadata. functional_traits <- data.table::fread( cmd = "xz -dc data/mag_gift_functions.tsv.xz", data.table = FALSE, check.names = FALSE ) stopifnot(identical(functional_traits$genome_id, genome_metadata$genome_id)) rownames(functional_traits) <- functional_traits$genome_id functional_traits$genome_id <- NULL # Protein degradation is defined by MEROPS peptidase families, which KEGG # annotation cannot supply, so it is zero in every MAG and carries no signal. empty_functions <- colnames(functional_traits)[colSums(functional_traits) == 0] functional_traits <- functional_traits[, !colnames(functional_traits) %in% empty_functions, drop = FALSE] stopifnot(identical(empty_functions, "D04"), all(as.matrix(functional_traits) >= 0 & as.matrix(functional_traits) <= 1)) function_labels <- unique(distillR::GIFT_db[c("Code_function", "Function", "Domain")]) function_labels <- function_labels[match(colnames(functional_traits), function_labels$Code_function), ] stopifnot(!anyNA(function_labels$Function)) cat(sprintf("%d MAGs, %d function-level traits (%d biosynthesis, %d degradation).\n", nrow(functional_traits), ncol(functional_traits), sum(function_labels$Domain == "Biosynthesis"), sum(function_labels$Domain == "Degradation"))) 5518 MAGs, 17 function-level traits (9 biosynthesis, 8 degradation). 7.2 Functional distance traits2dist() converts the trait table to a Gower distance, the mean absolute difference in completeness across traits, scaled to the range of each trait. Two MAGs with identical traits are at distance zero. functional_dist <- hilldiv3::traits2dist(functional_traits, method = "gower") stopifnot(identical(dim(functional_dist), c(5518L, 5518L)), all(is.finite(functional_dist))) dimnames(functional_dist) <- list(genome_metadata$genome_id, genome_metadata$genome_id) pair_distance <- functional_dist[upper.tri(functional_dist)] distance_quantiles <- stats::quantile(pair_distance, c(0.01, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99, 1)) knitr::kable( data.frame(Statistic = c("1%", "25%", "Median", "75%", "99%", "Maximum"), Distance = unname(distance_quantiles)), digits = 3 ) Statistic Distance 1% 0.087 25% 0.153 Median 0.188 75% 0.234 99% 0.452 Maximum 0.749 Quantiles of the pairwise functional distance between the 5,518 representatives. Functional Hill numbers count the effective number of functionally distinct types in a sample. Two MAGs closer than a threshold \(\tau\) count as largely the same type. We set \(\tau\) to the mean pairwise distance, 0.20, and examine how sensitive the results are to this choice below. functional_tau <- mean(pair_distance) 7.3 Functional diversity within samples We calculate neutral and functional Hill numbers at \(q=0\), \(q=1\) and \(q=2\) from the same abundances. A dist supplied with type = "functional" adds the functional layer. fd_neutral <- hilldiv3::hilldiv( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), type = "neutral" ) fd_functional <- hilldiv3::hilldiv( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), dist = functional_dist, tau = functional_tau, type = "functional" ) ggplot2::ggplot(fd_alpha, ggplot2::aes(x = value, y = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.55, fill = "#c9d8e8", colour = "#1f4e79") + ggplot2::geom_jitter(height = 0.13, width = 0, alpha = 0.28, size = 0.65, colour = "#1f4e79") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(type, order), ncol = 3, scales = "free_x") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Hill diversity", y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Neutral and functional Hill numbers for 45 samples in each habitat class. Horizontal scales differ by panel. fd_q1 <- fd_alpha[fd_alpha$q == 1, ] fd_wide <- reshape( fd_q1[c("sample", "habitat", "type", "value")], idvar = c("sample", "habitat"), timevar = "type", direction = "wide" ) names(fd_wide) <- sub("value\\.", "", names(fd_wide)) fd_wide$Redundancy <- fd_wide$Neutral / fd_wide$Functional fd_summary <- function(x) { sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", median(x), unname(quantile(x, 0.25)), unname(quantile(x, 0.75))) } fd_table <- data.frame( Habitat = habitat_levels, Neutral = tapply(fd_wide$Neutral, fd_wide$habitat, fd_summary)[habitat_levels], Functional = tapply(fd_wide$Functional, fd_wide$habitat, fd_summary)[habitat_levels], Redundancy = tapply(fd_wide$Redundancy, fd_wide$habitat, fd_summary)[habitat_levels] ) rownames(fd_table) <- NULL knitr::kable(fd_table, col.names = c("Habitat", "Neutral q = 1", "Functional q = 1", "Functional redundancy")) Habitat Neutral q = 1 Functional q = 1 Functional redundancy Agricultural field soil 47.8 [41.2–58.8] 5.3 [5.1–5.5] 9.3 [7.6–11.2] Natural grassland soil 55.1 [38.9–67.3] 5.0 [4.8–5.4] 11.1 [7.5–13.1] Natural forest soil 74.5 [47.9–107.0] 5.3 [5.1–5.4] 13.8 [9.9–19.4] Urban greenspace soil 48.4 [39.1–64.9] 5.3 [5.2–5.6] 9.0 [7.6–11.9] Natural bog/fen soil 52.7 [35.6–67.6] 4.8 [4.3–5.2] 11.3 [9.1–13.2] Natural freshwater sediment 50.6 [32.8–73.2] 4.9 [4.5–5.3] 10.6 [7.7–14.8] Natural saltwater sediment 48.3 [37.4–65.7] 4.3 [3.6–4.5] 11.5 [9.5–15.4] Urban wastewater water 78.0 [66.6–93.6] 6.2 [5.8–6.5] 12.9 [11.2–15.8] Median [interquartile range] of \(q=1\) diversity by habitat. Functional redundancy is neutral divided by functional diversity: the number of effective MAGs per effective functional type. At \(q=1\), median functional diversity ranges from 4.3 in Natural saltwater sediment to 6.2 in Urban wastewater water, while neutral diversity ranges from 48 to 78 effective MAGs. 7.4 Sensitivity to the distance threshold Functional Hill numbers depend on \(\tau\). A small \(\tau\) treats nearly every MAG as distinct and approaches neutral diversity; a large \(\tau\) merges them into a few functional types. We repeat the \(q=1\) calculation across a range of thresholds. tau_values <- sort(unique(c(0.1, 0.15, functional_tau, 0.3, 0.4))) tau_results <- lapply(tau_values, function(tau) { res <- plain_result(hilldiv3::hilldiv( overview_abundance, q = 1, dist = functional_dist, tau = tau, type = "functional" )) res$tau <- tau res }) tau_data <- do.call(rbind, tau_results) tau_data$habitat <- sample_metadata$habitat_label[ match(tau_data$sample, sample_metadata$sample_id) ] stopifnot(!anyNA(tau_data$habitat), all(is.finite(tau_data$value))) tau_median <- aggregate(value ~ habitat + tau, data = tau_data, FUN = median) tau_median$habitat <- factor(tau_median$habitat, levels = habitat_levels) ggplot2::ggplot(tau_median, ggplot2::aes(x = tau, y = value, colour = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.2) + ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = functional_tau, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors( length(habitat_levels), palette = "Dark 3")) + ggplot2::scale_y_log10() + ggplot2::labs(x = expression("Distance threshold" ~ tau), y = "Median functional Hill diversity, q = 1 (log scale)", colour = "Habitat") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) Median functional diversity per habitat across thresholds. The dashed line is the mean pairwise distance used elsewhere in this chapter. The habitat with the highest median functional diversity is Urban wastewater water at 5 of the 5 thresholds tested. 7.5 Community-level trait profiles The abundance-weighted mean completeness of each function in a sample, the community-weighted mean (CWM), describes the average functional capacity of the community without any threshold. It weights each MAG by its relative abundance within the profile. relative_profiles <- sweep(overview_abundance, 2, colSums(overview_abundance), "/") cwm <- t(relative_profiles) %*% as.matrix(functional_traits) stopifnot(identical(rownames(cwm), sample_metadata$sample_id), all(cwm >= -1e-10 & cwm <= 1 + 1e-10)) cwm_habitat <- aggregate(as.data.frame(cwm), by = list(habitat = sample_metadata$habitat_label), FUN = mean) cwm_long <- reshape( cwm_habitat, direction = "long", idvar = "habitat", varying = colnames(cwm), v.names = "cwm", timevar = "code", times = colnames(cwm) ) cwm_long$label <- paste(cwm_long$code, function_labels$Function[match(cwm_long$code, function_labels$Code_function)]) cwm_long$domain <- function_labels$Domain[match(cwm_long$code, function_labels$Code_function)] cwm_long$habitat <- factor(cwm_long$habitat, levels = habitat_levels) ggplot2::ggplot(cwm_long, ggplot2::aes(x = habitat, y = label, fill = cwm)) + ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white") + ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", cwm)), size = 2.6) + ggplot2::facet_grid(rows = ggplot2::vars(domain), scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") + ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(low = "#ffffff", high = "#c9784a", limits = c(0, 1)) + ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(guide = ggplot2::guide_axis(angle = 35)) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Mean CWM\ncompleteness") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Mean community-weighted completeness of each function across the 45 samples of a habitat. Values range from zero (no MAG carries the function) to one (the community is dominated by MAGs with the complete function). The function that differs most between habitats is B08 Aromatic compound biosynthesis, from 0.46 in Urban wastewater water to 0.66 in Natural forest soil. 7.6 Partitioning functional diversity hillpart() partitions functional diversity across samples, habitat classes and the full panel, as for neutral and phylogenetic diversity in the diversity chapter. functional_metadata <- data.frame( habitat_class = sample_metadata$habitat_class, row.names = sample_metadata$sample_id ) partition_functional <- hilldiv3::hillpart( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), dist = functional_dist, tau = functional_tau, hierarchy = ~ habitat_class, metadata = functional_metadata, type = "functional" ) partition_functional <- plain_result(partition_functional) stopifnot(all(is.finite(partition_functional$diversity))) f_within <- partition_functional[partition_functional$scale == "habitat_class", c("q", "beta")] f_total <- partition_functional[partition_functional$scale == "total", c("q", "beta", "diversity")] f_alpha <- partition_functional[partition_functional$scale == "sample", c("q", "diversity")] names(f_alpha)[2] <- "Alpha diversity" names(f_within)[2] <- "Within habitats" names(f_total)[2:3] <- c("Between habitats", "Gamma diversity") partition_functional_table <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "q"), list(f_alpha, f_within, f_total)) knitr::kable(partition_functional_table, digits = 2) q Alpha diversity Within habitats Between habitats Gamma diversity 0 8.05 1.00 1.00 8.08 1 6.39 1.06 1.03 6.99 2 5.67 1.09 1.05 6.45 Hierarchical partition of functional Hill numbers. Beta factors describe sample-to-habitat and habitat-to-panel turnover. At \(q=1\) the functional beta factors are 1.06 from samples to habitats and 1.03 from habitats to the full panel. These are much closer to one than the neutral and phylogenetic factors: communities in different habitats consist of different MAGs but carry largely overlapping functions. 7.7 Pairwise functional dissimilarity hillpair() compares every pair of samples, using the functional layer. As in the pairwise chapter, we use the C dissimilarity, here at \(q=1\). pair_functional <- hilldiv3::hillpair( overview_abundance, q = 1, metric = "C", dist = functional_dist, tau = functional_tau, type = "functional", out = "tibble" ) pair_functional <- plain_result(pair_functional) fd_ids <- sample_metadata$sample_id fd_first <- match(pair_functional$first, fd_ids) fd_second <- match(pair_functional$second, fd_ids) stopifnot(nrow(pair_functional) == choose(length(fd_ids), 2L), !anyNA(fd_first), !anyNA(fd_second), all(fd_first < fd_second), all(is.finite(pair_functional$value)), all(pair_functional$value >= -1e-10 & pair_functional$value <= 1 + 1e-10)) pair_functional$comparison <- ifelse( sample_metadata$habitat_label[fd_first] == sample_metadata$habitat_label[fd_second], "Within habitat", "Between habitats" ) pair_summary <- aggregate( value ~ comparison, data = pair_functional, FUN = function(x) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f–%.2f]", median(x), unname(quantile(x, 0.25)), unname(quantile(x, 0.75))) ) knitr::kable(pair_summary, col.names = c("Pairs", "Functional C, q = 1"), row.names = FALSE) Pairs Functional C, q = 1 Between habitats 0.07 [0.04–0.12] Within habitat 0.03 [0.01–0.07] Median [interquartile range] of functional C dissimilarity. Zero means identical functional communities and one means no functional overlap. ggplot2::ggplot(fd_points, ggplot2::aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, colour = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 1.5) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors( length(habitat_levels), palette = "Dark 3")) + ggplot2::labs(x = sprintf("PCoA 1 (%.1f%%)", fd_variance[1]), y = sprintf("PCoA 2 (%.1f%%)", fd_variance[2]), colour = "Habitat") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) Each point is one sample. Axis percentages are the shares of positive eigenvalues after the Cailliez correction. 7.8 Functional view of the Actinomycetota turnover The shares chapter found a nearly stable Actinomycetota total in agricultural field and natural grassland soils, with more Gaiellales in fields and more Streptosporangiales in grasslands. Do these two orders carry different functions, so that the swap changes what the community can do? We answer at the finer element level, such as individual amino acids, sugars or vitamins, which resolves more than the 17 function-level traits above. element_traits <- data.table::fread( cmd = "xz -dc data/mag_gift_elements.tsv.xz", data.table = FALSE, check.names = FALSE ) stopifnot(identical(element_traits$genome_id, genome_metadata$genome_id)) rownames(element_traits) <- element_traits$genome_id element_traits$genome_id <- NULL element_traits <- element_traits[, colSums(element_traits) > 0, drop = FALSE] element_matrix <- as.matrix(element_traits) element_labels <- unique(distillR::GIFT_db[c("Code_element", "Element", "Function")]) element_labels <- element_labels[match(colnames(element_matrix), element_labels$Code_element), ] element_labels$label <- sprintf("%s %s (%s)", element_labels$Code_element, element_labels$Element, tolower(element_labels$Function)) stopifnot(!anyNA(element_labels$Element)) element_dist <- hilldiv3::traits2dist(element_traits, method = "gower") dimnames(element_dist) <- list(genome_metadata$genome_id, genome_metadata$genome_id) element_tau <- mean(element_dist[upper.tri(element_dist)]) traits2dist() now uses the 161 of 170 elements that are present in at least one MAG (the others, including the protein-degradation elements, are absent from every MAG). We again set \(\tau\) to the mean pairwise distance, 0.22. The four disjoint sets are the two orders, the remaining Actinomycetota, and everything outside the phylum. They cover all representatives, so contributions add up to the total. We compare the mean field and grassland profiles, as in the dissimilarity analysis of the shares chapter. actino_ids <- genome_metadata$genome_id[phylum == "Actinomycetota"] fa_sets <- lapply(actino_orders, function(name) { actino_ids[genome_metadata[match(actino_ids, genome_metadata$genome_id), "order"] == paste0("o__", name)] }) names(fa_sets) <- actino_orders fa_sets[["Remaining Actinomycetota"]] <- setdiff(actino_ids, unlist(fa_sets)) fa_sets[["Outside Actinomycetota"]] <- setdiff(genome_metadata$genome_id, actino_ids) stopifnot(all(lengths(fa_sets) > 0L), sum(lengths(fa_sets)) == nrow(genome_metadata), setequal(unlist(fa_sets, use.names = FALSE), genome_metadata$genome_id)) fa_profiles <- function(field, grassland) { out <- cbind(rowMeans(overview_abundance[, field, drop = FALSE]), rowMeans(overview_abundance[, grassland, drop = FALSE])) colnames(out) <- contrast_habitats out } fa_field <- sample_metadata$habitat_label == contrast_habitats[1] fa_grass <- sample_metadata$habitat_label == contrast_habitats[2] fa_matched <- sample_metadata$project_id %in% c("P01_1", "P02_1") 7.8.1 Functional dissimilarity and the contribution of each set hillcontrib() splits the \(q=1\) C dissimilarity between the two mean profiles into contributions from each set. Neutral dissimilarity uses abundances alone; functional dissimilarity adds the element distance, so MAGs with similar elements count as the same functional type. fa_mean <- fa_profiles(fa_field, fa_grass) fa_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( fa_mean, q = 1, metric = "C", type = "neutral", sets = fa_sets ) fa_functional <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( fa_mean, q = 1, metric = "C", dist = element_dist, tau = element_tau, type = "functional", sets = fa_sets ) fa_plot <- rbind( data.frame(type = "Neutral", fa_neutral[c("set", "share")]), data.frame(type = "Functional (elements)", fa_functional[c("set", "share")]) ) fa_plot$set <- factor(fa_plot$set, levels = rev(c( actino_orders, "Remaining Actinomycetota", "Outside Actinomycetota" ))) fa_plot$type <- factor(fa_plot$type, levels = c("Neutral", "Functional (elements)")) ggplot2::ggplot(fa_plot, ggplot2::aes(x = share, y = type, fill = set)) + ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.6, colour = "white") + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c( Gaiellales = "#9d2f30", Streptosporangiales = "#d4846e", `Remaining Actinomycetota` = "#a6a6a6", `Outside Actinomycetota` = "#e6dcd0" ), breaks = c(actino_orders, "Remaining Actinomycetota", "Outside Actinomycetota")) + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Share of C dissimilarity", y = NULL, fill = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom") Share of the \(q=1\) C dissimilarity between mean field and grassland profiles attributed to each set, for abundance alone (neutral) and with the element distance (functional). Neutral C between the two mean profiles is 0.285, while functional C is only 0.010 at this threshold: most of the abundance turnover replaces MAGs with similar elements. Gaiellales and Streptosporangiales hold only 3.2% of the representatives, yet they account for 19% of the neutral and 36% of the functional dissimilarity. The two orders therefore explain a larger part of the functional turnover than of the abundance turnover. fa_robust_table <- data.frame( fa_robust$Comparison, sprintf("%.3f", fa_robust$neutral), sprintf("%.3f", fa_robust$functional), sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * fa_robust$share_neutral), sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * fa_robust$share_functional) ) knitr::kable(fa_robust_table, col.names = c( "Comparison", "Neutral C", "Functional C", "Orders' share of neutral C", "Orders' share of functional C" )) Comparison Neutral C Functional C Orders’ share of neutral C Orders’ share of functional C All samples, mean tau 0.285 0.010 19% 36% All samples, tau = 0.10 0.285 0.214 19% 23% All samples, tau = 0.40 0.285 0.000 19% 27% Project-matched samples, mean tau 0.314 0.014 23% 55% Higher-quality MAGs only, mean tau 0.264 0.013 12% 18% Functional dissimilarity depends on \(\tau\) (a small threshold approaches the neutral value, a large one removes it), so it is shown for three thresholds, for the 16 field and 7 grassland samples that share projects, as in the shares chapter, and for MAGs with CheckM2 completeness of at least 80% and contamination of at most 10%. The orders’ larger share of functional dissimilarity holds in every row, but its margin is smallest among the higher-quality MAGs. 7.8.2 Do the two orders offset each other? For each element we split the field-minus-grassland difference in community-weighted mean completeness into the part contributed by each set. Positive values mean higher completeness in fields. If the swap between orders left the community’s functions unchanged, Gaiellales and Streptosporangiales would contribute opposite amounts for every element. fa_by_set <- fa_decompose(fa_mean) fa_elements <- data.frame( code = rownames(fa_by_set), fa_by_set, check.names = FALSE, label = element_labels$label[match(rownames(fa_by_set), element_labels$Code_element)] ) fa_elements$orders <- fa_elements$Gaiellales + fa_elements$Streptosporangiales fa_elements$total <- rowSums(fa_by_set) stopifnot(!anyNA(fa_elements$label)) fa_top <- fa_elements[order(-abs(fa_elements$orders)), ][1:12, ] ggplot2::ggplot(fa_elements, ggplot2::aes(x = Gaiellales, y = Streptosporangiales)) + ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") + ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = -1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") + ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#702626", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Gaiellales contribution", y = "Streptosporangiales contribution") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) Each point is one element. The dashed line marks complete offset: the two orders contribute equal and opposite amounts. The contributions of the two orders are negatively correlated across the 161 elements (r = -0.78). Summed over elements, their absolute contributions are 4.1 times larger than the absolute contribution of the two orders combined, so most of what one order adds is cancelled by the other. The offset is partial: the two orders together still shift the completeness of individual elements. fa_top_long <- rbind( data.frame(label = fa_top$label, set = "Gaiellales", value = fa_top$Gaiellales), data.frame(label = fa_top$label, set = "Streptosporangiales", value = fa_top$Streptosporangiales) ) fa_top_long$label <- factor(fa_top_long$label, levels = rev(fa_top$label)) fa_top$label <- factor(fa_top$label, levels = rev(fa_top$label)) ggplot2::ggplot(fa_top_long, ggplot2::aes(x = value, y = label)) + ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") + ggplot2::geom_col(ggplot2::aes(fill = set), position = "dodge", width = 0.7) + ggplot2::geom_point(data = fa_top, ggplot2::aes(x = orders, y = label), shape = 18, size = 3) + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(Gaiellales = "#9d2f30", Streptosporangiales = "#d4846e")) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Contribution to field minus grassland mean completeness", y = NULL, fill = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom") The twelve elements with the largest net effect of the two orders. Bars are the contribution of each order; the diamond is their sum. The largest net effect is for D0908 Macrolide (antibiotic degradation): Gaiellales contributes +0.053 and Streptosporangiales -0.004, so the orders together shift it by +0.049. Of these 12 elements, 9 are degradation elements for which Streptosporangiales, enriched in grasslands, raises grassland completeness. The replacement of Gaiellales by Streptosporangiales is therefore not functionally neutral at the level of individual elements, even though the overall functional dissimilarity is small. 7.9 Trait validation and sensitivity to MAG quality Before relying on the traits we check that they behave as expected for clades whose metabolism is well known, and that the main results do not simply track how complete a MAG is. validation_phyla <- names(which(table(phylum) >= 60L)) validation_codes <- c("B01", "B02", "B07", "D02") validation <- t(vapply(validation_phyla, function(name) { colMeans(functional_traits[phylum == name, validation_codes]) }, numeric(length(validation_codes)))) validation <- validation[order(-validation[, "D02"]), ] antibiotic_max <- max(vapply(validation_phyla, function(name) { mean(functional_traits[phylum == name, "B10"]) }, numeric(1))) stopifnot(antibiotic_max < 0.05) colnames(validation) <- function_labels$Function[ match(validation_codes, function_labels$Code_function) ] knitr::kable(validation, digits = 2) Nucleic acid biosynthesis Amino acid biosynthesis Vitamin biosynthesis Polysaccharide degradation Acidobacteriota 0.84 0.58 0.46 0.45 Planctomycetota 0.81 0.58 0.43 0.38 Bacteroidota 0.81 0.46 0.39 0.35 Verrucomicrobiota 0.66 0.54 0.48 0.35 Chloroflexota 0.65 0.45 0.27 0.31 Actinomycetota 0.78 0.59 0.42 0.28 Bacillota 0.77 0.49 0.36 0.26 Cyanobacteriota 0.83 0.66 0.62 0.24 Pseudomonadota 0.82 0.65 0.48 0.19 Desulfobacterota 0.75 0.61 0.47 0.11 Patescibacteria 0.35 0.03 0.02 0.06 Halobacteriota 0.79 0.53 0.32 0.05 Thermoproteota 0.67 0.33 0.29 0.04 Mean completeness of four functions among the phyla with at least 60 representatives. The patterns match expectations. Patescibacteria, whose reduced genomes depend on other cells, score near zero for amino acid (0.03) and vitamin (0.02) biosynthesis, and well below the other phyla for nucleic acids (0.35 against at least 0.65). Polysaccharide degradation is highest in Acidobacteriota, Planctomycetota, Bacteroidota, groups known for degrading complex carbohydrates, and lowest in Thermoproteota. KEGG orthologs do not resolve antibiotic biosynthesis: it stays below 0.05 in every phylum, including the Actinomycetota. trait_cors <- vapply(c("genome_size", "checkm2_completeness"), function(v) { stats::median(abs(vapply(colnames(functional_traits), function(f) { stats::cor(functional_traits[[f]], genome_metadata[[v]], method = "spearman") }, numeric(1)))) }, numeric(1)) Trait completeness rises with genome size and CheckM2 completeness: the median absolute Spearman correlation across the 17 functions is 0.54 with genome size and 0.21 with completeness. Larger genomes do carry more metabolic functions, but incomplete MAGs also miss genes, so trait values are lower bounds. To see whether the conclusions depend on this, we repeat the analyses with the 3186 representatives that have CheckM2 completeness of at least 80% and contamination of at most 10%, renormalizing each profile. quality_profiles <- overview_abundance[quality_keep, , drop = FALSE] quality_profiles <- sweep(quality_profiles, 2, colSums(quality_profiles), "/") quality_dist <- functional_dist[quality_keep, quality_keep] quality_functional <- hilldiv3::hilldiv( quality_profiles, q = 1, dist = quality_dist, tau = mean(quality_dist[upper.tri(quality_dist)]), type = "functional" ) quality_functional <- plain_result(quality_functional) quality_medians <- tapply( quality_functional$value, sample_metadata$habitat_label[match(quality_functional$sample, sample_metadata$sample_id)], median )[habitat_levels] all_medians <- tapply(fd_wide$Functional, fd_wide$habitat, median)[habitat_levels] quality_cwm <- t(quality_profiles) %*% as.matrix(functional_traits[quality_keep, ]) cwm_agreement <- vapply(colnames(cwm), function(f) { stats::cor(tapply(cwm[, f], sample_metadata$habitat_label, mean)[habitat_levels], tapply(quality_cwm[, f], sample_metadata$habitat_label, mean)[habitat_levels], method = "spearman") }, numeric(1)) knitr::kable( data.frame(Habitat = habitat_levels, `All MAGs` = unname(all_medians), `Higher-quality MAGs` = unname(quality_medians), check.names = FALSE), digits = 2 ) Habitat All MAGs Higher-quality MAGs Agricultural field soil 5.26 3.65 Natural grassland soil 5.05 3.62 Natural forest soil 5.28 3.78 Urban greenspace soil 5.31 3.70 Natural bog/fen soil 4.77 3.43 Natural freshwater sediment 4.85 3.73 Natural saltwater sediment 4.26 3.37 Urban wastewater water 6.20 5.52 Median functional diversity (\(q=1\)) per habitat with all representatives and with the higher-quality subset. Each uses its own mean pairwise distance as \(\tau\). The subset holds a median of 62% of each sample’s profile. Absolute functional diversity is lower, but the habitat ranking is similar (Spearman 0.81) and Urban wastewater water remains highest. The habitat means of the community-weighted trait profiles agree between the two sets (median Spearman 0.95 across functions, minimum 0.69). Within the Actinomycetota analysis, the higher-quality row of the robustness table keeps the negative correlation between the orders (r = -0.72) and a small functional dissimilarity, but the orders’ share of functional dissimilarity falls to 18% against 12% neutral. We therefore read that excess as a modest, not a large, effect. 7.10 Interpretation and limits These traits come from gene presence in KEGG ortholog annotations. They describe genomic potential, not expressed activity, and cover only functions that KEGG orthologs and EC numbers can define. Protein degradation, which needs MEROPS peptidase families, is left out. Each representative’s abundance stands for its 95% ANI cluster, which need not share its gene content. Functional diversity depends on the trait set and on \(\tau\); compare values only within one choice of both. The pairwise and ordination summaries describe this selected panel. Pairs sharing samples are dependent, and habitat class is partly confounded with sampling year, so none of these comparisons is a formal test of a habitat effect. Relative abundances also cannot support read-count rarefaction or sampling-depth uncertainty estimates.
